prime.problem: "99.9%" sounds like a quality, not a budget, so teams give every part the same target, add copies without asking what they share, and discover in the first incident that a 60-minute manual failover spends the whole month's 43.2 minutes at once.
prime.fits: Third estimation card. Back-of-envelope turned rates into what's in flight; this card turns an availability target into minutes, and shows how parts in series and copies in parallel combine. cs-5 picks up where the independence assumption breaks.
expect: uptime vs yield, MTTF and MTTR
prime.goal: Convert any target to minutes and requests, budget it along a request path, and say when adding copies stops helping.

attend: Why does each extra nine divide the downtime budget by exactly 10?
Why do 20 parts at 99.99% miss a 99.9% target, and what must each part have instead?
Why does "2 of 3 servers at 99% each" miss 99.99%, and what per-server availability does it need?
What does one shared 99.95% layer do to three independent copies?
Why can cutting repair time be cheaper than preventing failures?

must: Availability target → allowed downtime = (1 − A) × T → 99.9% of a 30-day month = 43.2 min → a single 60-minute failover spends the budget at once → recovery time must be checked against the budget

A request needs every part on its path → availabilities multiply → 20 parts at 99.99% = 0.998 = 86.3 min a month → parts need more nines than the whole (the source's 99.99% API tier under a 99.9% service)

Copies where any one is enough → failure chances multiply (1 − 0.01³) → huge gains, but only if copies fail independently → a shared layer in series sets the floor (21.6 min at 99.95%), which is why "replicate until pᴺ < R" is hogwash

A = MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR) → the same target can be met by failing less or recovering faster → at 99.9%, a 2-minute automatic failover needs a failure-free stretch of only 1.39 days vs 41.6 days for a 60-minute manual one
elevated: Time availability counts a second at 3 a.m. the same as a second at peak → yield (share of requests served) weights outages by traffic → at 10K RPS the 99.9% budget is 25,920,000 failed requests a month
reference: the full nines table in minutes and hours

compress.prompt: From memory, write the three rules (budget, serial, parallel) with one TinyURL-sized example each, and add one sentence on why copies stop helping.
checklist: D = (1 − A) × T: 43.2 min a month at 99.9%
parallel: 1 − (1 − p)ᵏ; three 99% copies → 2.6 s a month
only if copies fail independently; a shared layer sets the floor
budget in time or in requests; repair time counts as much as failure rate

retrieve.q: Explain why the source sets the API tier one nine stricter (99.99%) than the whole service (99.9%).
answer: the API is only one of several parts a request passes through
availabilities multiply along the path, so the total is lower than any part
0.999 / 0.9999 ≈ 0.9991 leaves 38.9 min a month for queue, auth and workers

retrieve.q: Walk through the "2 of 3 servers at 99% each" calculation and say whether it meets 99.99%.
answer: P(all 3 up) = p³; P(exactly 2 up) = 3p²(1 − p)
12.9 min a month: misses 99.99% (4.32 min); each server needs p ≥ 0.99422

retrieve.q: You can spend next quarter either adding a fourth copy or automating failover. Using the card's numbers, which is likely the better use of time, and why?
answer: a third copy already saves only minutes; the shared layer (21.6 min) dominates
one manual 60-minute failover spends more than the whole 43.2-minute budget
automating repair cuts MTTR, which the card says is often cheaper than preventing failures

compare.q: This card's parallel formula assumes independent copies; cs-5's correlated-failure card is about when they aren't. What does the shared failure chance c do to 1 − pᴺ, and how should that change what you build?
answer: the shared chance c doesn't shrink as N grows
it sets a floor on unavailability, so adding copies stops helping
spend on removing shared fate (separate configs, power, rollouts) rather than on more copies

compare.q: Uptime vs yield is a choice of average. Which average does each measure take, and when would they tell different stories?
answer: uptime averages over time: every second counts equally
yield averages over requests: busy seconds count more
they differ when outages hit peak traffic (yield worse) or quiet nights (uptime worse)

predict.q: Your read path has 3 parts at 99.95% each, then a database pair where either copy is enough, each at 99.9%. Before computing: does the path meet 99.9%, and which piece dominates the downtime?
predict.answer: It misses. The pair gives 1 − 0.001² = 0.999999, so it's nearly free. The three serial parts give 0.9995³ ≈ 0.9985, about 64.8 min a month against a 43.2-minute budget. The serial chain dominates, so another database copy wouldn't help; fewer or better serial parts would.

apply.task: Budget TinyURL's read path: the course's 99.9% target over a 30-day month. The path has a load balancer, an app server and a cache, each at 99.99%, and a database at 99.95%. (1) Compute the path's availability and monthly downtime. (2) Say how many minutes are left for incidents. (3) At 99.95% with 10-minute repairs, compute how long the database must run between failures.
apply.done: You get 0.9999³ × 0.9995 ≈ 0.99920 (about 34.5 min of expected downtime a month, leaving about 8.7 min), and MTTF = 10 × 0.9995 / 0.0005 ≈ 19,990 min ≈ 13.9 days.
apply.hint: From A = MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR), MTTF = MTTR × A / (1 − A).

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: which piece dominated the path's downtime?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why serial parts need more nines than the whole?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: copies → multiplied failure chances, or shared layer → floor?
Where in a system you know does a shared dependency quietly sit in series with all the copies?
What will you look for in cs-5's correlated-failure card?
